item.title: Migrating to stateless MCP: a playbook for the 2026-07-28 specification
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The MCP 2026-07-28 spec removed sessions and the handshake. A playbook for migrating servers, gateways and clients: state handles, MRTR, headers, caching and auth changes.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026-07-28 Model Context Protocol specification turned a stateful, bidirectional protocol into a stateless request and response one. That is good news for anyone running MCP servers at scale, and a real migration for anyone who built on sessions, server-initiated requests or long-lived streams.

Most early MCP servers were built like chat connections: a client connected, shook hands, held a session open and the server pushed requests back when it needed something. That worked on a laptop. It worked less well behind a load balancer, in serverless runtimes, or anywhere a connection could drop. The 2026-07-28 specification addresses that head on1.

What changed, in one table

BeforeFrom 2026-07-28Why it matters
initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-IdRemoved; each request carries protocol version and client capabilities in _metaAny request can land on any instance2
Capabilities learned at connect timeOptional server/discover call that servers must implementUp-front version selection when clients want it2
Server-initiated elicitation, sampling and roots requestsMulti Round-Trip Requests: the server returns input_required and the client retries with answersNo held-open bidirectional stream3
Method and tool names only in the JSON bodyMcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers required on Streamable HTTPGateways route and authorise on headers4
List results with no freshness hintsttlMs and cacheScope, plus deterministic tool orderClient caching and stable prompt caches2
SSE resumability with Last-Event-IDRemoved; a broken stream means re-issuing the requestSimpler transport, but retries must be safe2

The release also moved Tasks into an official extension, hardened authorisation with RFC 9207 issuer validation, deprecated Dynamic Client Registration in favour of client metadata documents, and introduced a formal deprecation policy with a twelve-month minimum window1.

The playbook

1. Inventory what depends on sessions

List every server and find where it relies on connection state: per-session caches, "current project" set at connect time, server-pushed requests, resumable streams. Those are your migration items. Servers that only expose stateless tools usually need little more than an SDK upgrade.

2. Replace hidden state with explicit handles

The specification's answer to cross-call state is an explicit, server-minted handle returned by a tool and passed back as an ordinary argument2. The maintainers note this works better than transport-hidden state because the model can see the handle and thread it between tools1. Store the state behind the handle in a shared store, scoped to the user, with an expiry.

3. Rework interactive tools with MRTR

Tools that asked the user for confirmation or a missing parameter mid-call now return an interim result with resultType: "input_required"; the client gathers the answers and retries the original request with them3. Design these tools so a retry is safe, and keep any correlation data in the request state rather than server memory.

4. Make retries safe everywhere

Without stream resumability, a dropped response stream means the client re-issues the request with a new ID2. Any tool with side effects needs idempotency, the same discipline as in idempotent payment pipelines.

5. Move routing and policy to the gateway

With Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name on every Streamable HTTP request4, a gateway can rate-limit, authorise and meter per tool without parsing bodies. Plain round-robin load balancing now works. This is the natural place to enforce the controls in securing MCP servers.

6. Use the cache hints

Return a deterministic tool order and sensible ttlMs values. Stable tool lists help clients cache catalogues and keep upstream prompt caches warm, which matters for cost, as covered in prompt caching.

7. Plan the deprecations

Roots, Sampling and Logging are deprecated, with suggested migrations: pass paths through tool parameters or configuration instead of Roots, call model providers directly instead of Sampling, and use stderr or OpenTelemetry instead of protocol Logging25. Trace context now has documented conventions in _meta, which fits the approach in LLM observability.

Stateless MCP doesn't make your system stateless. It makes your state visible, which is exactly where an auditor, an SRE and the model all need it to be.

Sequencing for an enterprise estate

  1. Gateway first, so routing and policy work for both old and new protocol versions during the transition.
  2. High-traffic, stateless servers next: the easiest wins for scalability.
  3. Interactive and stateful servers last, with handles and MRTR designed and tested properly.
  4. Registry metadata updated to show which protocol versions each server supports, as in an enterprise MCP registry.

How I can help

item.title: Shipping AI features with evidence: a shared evaluation and observability platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a software company with many AI features can ship model and prompt changes safely: shared eval sets, release gates, OpenTelemetry GenAI tracing and cost per feature.
item.content:encoded:
Several product teams had shipped AI features, each with its own prompts, its own vendor calls and its own idea of 'good'. Model upgrades were risky, regressions were found by customers, and nobody could say what an AI feature cost to run. The goal was one platform for evaluating, releasing and observing every LLM feature.

The situation

A software company had moved quickly on AI. Support had an answer assistant, sales had an email drafter, the core product had a summariser and a natural-language search box. Each team had picked prompts, vendors and settings independently. When a model provider released a new version, nobody knew which features would get better and which would quietly break. Quality problems surfaced as customer tickets. Finance saw one large model invoice and could not split it by feature.

Leadership did not want to slow the teams down. They wanted the same confidence in AI releases that they already had in ordinary code releases.

What had to be true

  • Every AI feature has an evaluation set that reflects real use, owned by the team that ships it.
  • Changes ship through gates: a prompt, model or retrieval change runs the evals before it reaches customers.
  • Every model and tool call is traceable, with latency, tokens and errors, using an open standard rather than a vendor format.
  • Sensitive content is not logged by default.
  • Cost and quality are visible per feature, so product managers can make trade-offs.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

Tracing followed the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI, which standardise how model calls are recorded, including the model, input and output token counts and, when explicitly enabled, prompt and completion content12. Standard metrics for token usage and operation duration made cost and latency comparable across features and vendors3. The detail is in LLM observability with OpenTelemetry.

The hard part: evaluation sets that predict production

Building the pipeline was straightforward. Building evaluation sets that actually predicted how features behaved for customers was not. Generic benchmarks said little about whether the support assistant would answer a specific customer's question correctly.

  • Cases drawn from real, anonymised usage, grouped by intent, with a slice of known hard and sensitive cases.
  • Deterministic checks wherever possible: format, required fields, citations present, forbidden content absent.
  • Rubric-based model graders only where judgement was needed, calibrated against human labels. Research on LLM-as-a-judge found strong models can match human preference agreement, but also documented position and verbosity biases that need controlling4.
  • Regular refresh from production misses, so the set evolves with the product.

More on this in evaluation sets that predict production and, for agentic features, evaluating AI agents.

An eval set is a product artefact, not a test fixture. The team that owns the feature owns its definition of good.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
OpenTelemetry GenAI conventionsA vendor-specific tracing SDKPortable across vendors and backends, fits existing observability
Content capture off by defaultLog everything for debuggingPrompts and tool arguments can hold sensitive data
Deterministic checks before judgesJudge every output with a modelCheaper, faster and free of judge bias
Eval sets owned by feature teamsCentral QA writes all evalsTeams know what good looks like for their users
Gateway for all model callsEach team calls vendors directlyOne place for keys, routing, limits and cost attribution

The programme was mapped to the NIST Generative AI Profile, which gave the risk team a recognised structure for issues such as confabulation, information security and data privacy5.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with tracing and cost per feature, because visibility creates demand for evaluation. Differently: write a model upgrade playbook in the first phase. Provider version changes arrive on their schedule, not yours, and a rehearsed path from new model to gated rollout takes the drama out of them.

item.title: Characterisation on OMOP: describe your population before you predict or estimate anything
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Database profiles, cohort characterisation, treatment pathways and incidence rates on OMOP: what each tells you, how to compute them, and why they come before AI.
item.content:encoded:
Health data teams are under pressure to jump straight to prediction models and causal studies. The most useful first step is less glamorous: describing the data and the people in it. OHDSI's characterisation methods turn that into a repeatable, shareable discipline.

A familiar pattern in health data projects: the team gets access to a new OMOP database, and within a week someone is training a risk model. A month later the model behaves strangely, and the cause turns out to be something basic. Half the patients have under a year of observation, a whole drug class is missing from one source, or the "new users" are mostly people transferring in from another system.

Characterisation is how you find those things first. The Book of OHDSI describes four methods, each answering a different question1.

Four kinds of characterisation

MethodQuestion it answersTypical use
Database-levelWhat is in this database at all?Fitness for purpose, data quality, spotting gaps
Cohort characterisationWho are these people, before and after the index date?Natural history, drug utilisation, study feasibility
Treatment pathwaysWhat sequence of treatments do people receive?Treatment patterns, switching, guideline adherence
IncidenceHow often does a new outcome occur in a population?Disease burden, safety signals, baselines for models

All except database-level characterisation describe a population relative to an index date defined by a cohort. Time before the index date is baseline; the index date and after is post-index1. That is why good cohort definitions come first.

Start with the database

Before any population question, describe the database: how many people, their age distribution, how long they are observed, and how the recording of treatments, conditions and procedures changes over time. These summaries also reveal what may be missing1, which is why they pair naturally with OMOP data quality checks.

Characterise the cohort broadly

OHDSI's approach to cohort characterisation is deliberately broad: descriptive statistics across all conditions, drug and device exposures, procedures and other observations in a person's history, plus demographics at the index date. That gives a complete picture of the population and helps surface variation and missing values1. The FeatureExtraction package produces these features in a standard way, so the same characterisation runs at every site4.

The book notes that disseminating this kind of characterisation is recommended practice in the STROBE guidelines for reporting observational studies13. Practically, a baseline table is also the fastest way to check your cohort is the population you think it is.

If the baseline table surprises you, stop. The surprise is either a finding or a data problem, and both matter more than the model you were about to train.

Treatment pathways

Pathway analysis summarises the sequence of treatments people receive after a starting event, such as a diagnosis or first prescription. In a landmark study across the OHDSI network, Hripcsak and colleagues used standardised pathway analyses for type 2 diabetes, hypertension and depression, running the same analysis across many databases2. The book reports that they found metformin to be the most common diabetes medication, consistent with first-line guidance, and that 10% of diabetes patients, 24% of hypertension patients and 11% of depression patients followed a treatment pathway shared with no one else in any of the data sources1.

That last finding is a useful reminder for anyone designing clinical AI: real-world care is far more varied than guidelines suggest.

Incidence, defined precisely

Incidence measures new occurrences of an outcome in a population during a time at risk. The book defines two metrics1:

  • Incidence proportion: people in the cohort with a new outcome during the time at risk, divided by people in the cohort with time at risk.
  • Incidence rate: people with a new outcome divided by the total person-time at risk, where each person's time stops when the outcome occurs.

Most disagreements about "the rate" of something trace back to different choices of cohort, time at risk or outcome definition. Writing those down explicitly is what makes incidence comparable across sites and studies.

Where characterisation fits

  1. Database characterisation when a source joins the platform, and after every major load.
  2. Cohort characterisation before any study or model, to confirm feasibility and population.
  3. Pathways and incidence to understand current practice and baselines.
  4. Then prediction or effect estimation, with the characterisation published alongside the results.

How I can help

I design OMOP platforms where characterisation runs automatically on every load and every new cohort, so analysts and AI teams start from facts rather than assumptions. See healthcare data architecture, or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Making Kubernetes spend visible, owned and controllable, without slowing teams down
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a scale-up can make Kubernetes spend visible and controllable per team: cost allocation, right-sizing without restarts, scale to zero, quotas and a paved road.
item.content:encoded:
Cloud bills were growing faster than the business, and nobody could say which team or product drove the increase. The goal was a platform where every workload has an owner, a cost, sensible defaults and a cheap way to shrink, so cost becomes a product decision rather than a quarterly panic.

The situation

A fast-growing technology company ran most of its products on a handful of shared Kubernetes clusters. Teams shipped quickly, which was the point. But cloud spend had become one of the largest lines in the budget, and the monthly review was a guessing game: the bill showed compute, storage and network by account, while the organisation thought in teams and products. Requests and limits had been copied between services for years. Some workloads ran around the clock for jobs that happened once a day.

A previous clean-up project had cut costs for a quarter, then spend crept back. The leadership question was simple: how do we make this stay fixed?

What had to be true

  • Every workload has an owner: a team and a product, enforced, not hoped for.
  • Cost is visible where decisions are made: per team, per product, in a format finance accepts.
  • Efficiency is the default: new services start right-sized and autoscaled without teams becoming Kubernetes experts.
  • Shrinking is cheap and safe, so teams actually do it.
  • No slowdown in delivery; controls live in the paved road, not in tickets.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

OpenCost provides workload-level cost allocation for Kubernetes, attributing cluster costs to namespaces, labels and workloads1. Joining those allocations with billing data in the FinOps Foundation's FOCUS format gave finance and engineering one view of the same numbers2; the reasoning is in FOCUS and AI spend.

The hard part: making shrinking safe

Visibility alone rarely changes behaviour. Teams knew some services were over-provisioned; they left them because changing requests meant restarts, and restarts meant risk. Two Kubernetes changes removed most of that friction:

  • In-place Pod resize, stable since Kubernetes 1.35, lets CPU and memory change on running Pods, and the Vertical Pod Autoscaler's in-place mode uses it3. Recommendations could finally be applied continuously, starting with CPU on stateless services. Details in in-place Pod resize.
  • Scale to zero with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, available from Kubernetes 1.37 for workloads driven by suitable object or external metrics such as queue length4. Workers that waited idle most of the day stopped costing anything while idle. See Kubernetes FinOps and scale to zero.

Namespace quotas then capped the total each team could request, which turned capacity into a visible, negotiable budget rather than an unlimited pool5.

Cost programmes fail when saving money is risky and spending it is free. Flip both: make shrinking safe and automatic, and make every request visible to its owner.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Enforce ownership labels at admissionTag clean-up campaignsUnowned workloads can't appear in the first place
Open-source allocation plus FOCUSA separate cost tool per cloudOne allocation model and one billing schema across providers
Right-size in place, CPU firstRolling restarts for every changeLower risk, so recommendations actually get applied
Scale to zero only for queue-backed workScale everything to zeroUser-facing services need warm capacity
Quotas as team budgetsUnlimited shared poolMakes capacity a visible, negotiated decision

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with ownership and allocation, and put every improvement into the templates so it spreads automatically. Differently: agree unit cost metrics with product leaders earlier. Cost per team tells you who spends; cost per customer action tells you whether the spend is worth it.

item.title: From MCP servers on laptops to a governed enterprise agent platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an enterprise can move from ad hoc MCP servers on laptops to a governed agent platform: a private registry, central identity, scoped tokens, gateways and audit.
item.content:encoded:
Engineers had connected assistants to dozens of MCP servers, some internal, some from the internet, most with broad tokens. Security wanted to stop it; product teams wanted more of it. The goal was a platform that made the approved path the easiest one.

The situation

An organisation had embraced AI assistants faster than it had governed them. Developers connected IDE assistants to MCP servers for the code host, the ticketing system and the data warehouse. Some servers were built internally in an afternoon; others were installed from public repositories. Many used personal access tokens with wide permissions, stored in local configuration files. Nobody could say which servers were in use, who had approved them, or what they had done.

Security's first instinct was to block MCP outright. Leadership's instinct was the opposite: agents were becoming central to engineering and operations, and a ban would simply push usage further out of sight.

What had to be true

  • One place to find approved servers, discoverable by the clients people already use.
  • No long-lived shared tokens. Access flows through the identity provider, per user, with the narrowest scopes that work.
  • Every tool call is attributable to a person, an agent, a server and a version.
  • Writes and destructive actions need explicit, visible consent.
  • Publishing a new internal server is easy if it follows the standard; exceptions are rare and visible.

Architecture

The design followed the ecosystem's own shape: the official MCP Registry is intended as an upstream that organisations build private subregistries on, adding internal servers that should never appear publicly3. The approach is described in more depth in running an enterprise MCP registry.

The data flow, end to end

Step five matters most. The MCP security guidance names token passthrough, where a server forwards a token it received from the client to a downstream API, as an anti-pattern that breaks OAuth security boundaries, and the authorisation specification forbids it12. Every server on the platform validates that tokens were issued for it, and calls downstream systems with its own, separately scoped credentials.

The hard part: scopes people would actually accept

The technical controls were well understood. The difficult part was scope design. The MCP guidance warns that over-broad scopes granted up front expand the blast radius of a stolen token, make revocation disruptive and create consent dialogs that users abandon; it recommends a progressive, least-privilege model starting with a minimal read-only set1. In practice that meant:

  • A small, named set of scopes per server, starting with read-only discovery.
  • Write and admin scopes requested only when a user first invokes a tool that needs them.
  • Central control through the identity provider using the authorisation extensions, so administrators can grant and revoke access in one place4.
  • Metrics on which scopes are requested and used, so creep is visible.

Least privilege only works if the least-privilege path is also the least-friction path. Otherwise people find a personal token and work around it.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Private registry mirroring the public oneAllow-list in a wikiClients can discover from it, and versions can be pinned
Gateway in front of remote serversEach server enforces policy aloneOne place for authentication, policy, rate limits and audit
Servers use their own downstream credentialsPass client tokens throughToken passthrough is forbidden and breaks audit and audience checks
Progressive scopesGrant everything at first loginSmaller blast radius and consent people actually read
Enforce after migrationBlock first, build laterAvoids pushing usage underground

The prompt injection and excessive agency risks in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications shaped the server template, with tool descriptions treated as untrusted and write tools gated by consent5. The detailed controls are in securing MCP servers, prompt injection defence for agents and MCP extensions strategy.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with an inventory and make the approved path faster than the unapproved one before enforcing anything. Differently: publish the server template and its CI checks in the first phase. Teams wanted to build compliant servers early, and every week without a template produced another one-off that later needed migrating.

item.title: OpenTelemetry declarative configuration: a playbook for moving from environment variables to one reviewed file
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: OpenTelemetry's declarative configuration schema is stable. What changed, which languages support it, and a playbook for moving SDK setup from env vars to one reviewed file.
item.content:encoded:
For years, configuring OpenTelemetry SDKs meant a growing list of OTEL_ environment variables, plus code for anything they couldn't express. The declarative configuration schema is now stable. It turns telemetry setup into a versioned file that platform teams can standardise, review and roll out.

Ask a platform team how their services configure OpenTelemetry and the honest answer is usually "it depends on the service". One team sets a dozen OTEL_ variables in a Helm chart, another wires exporters in code, a third copied a sampler setting from a blog post two years ago. The result is telemetry that differs in quality across services for no good reason, and changes that require touching every repository.

OpenTelemetry's declarative configuration is designed to fix that, and the core of it is now stable.

What changed

In March 2026 the project marked key portions of the declarative configuration specification stable12:

  • The JSON schema for the data model, released as opentelemetry-configuration 1.0.03.
  • The YAML file format and the in-memory representation of the model.
  • The SDK operations to parse a file and create SDK components from it.
  • A standard environment variable, OTEL_CONFIG_FILE, to point the SDK at the file.

At the time, implementations existed in C++, Go, Java, JavaScript and PHP, with .NET and Python under way, and the Collector used the Go implementation for its own internal telemetry1. Since then, the Java Spring Boot starter has added support from version 2.26.0, embedding the same schema in application.yaml4.

Why it matters

Environment variables are flat. They can name an exporter endpoint, but struggle with a pipeline: several processors, different exporters per signal, views that drop noisy attributes, a sampler with rules. Anything beyond them meant code, or for the Java agent a separate extension jar4. The declarative schema describes the whole SDK pipeline as a tree, in the same shape the SDK runs5:

file_format: "1.0"
resource:
  attributes:
    - name: service.name
      value: checkout
tracer_provider:
  processors:
    - batch:
        exporter:
          otlp_http:
            endpoint: ${OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT:-http://collector:4318/v1/traces}

Environment variable substitution keeps the parts that genuinely vary per environment out of the file, while everything else becomes a reviewable artefact.

Telemetry configuration is platform policy. It belongs in one reviewed file per service type, not scattered across Helm values and application code.

The playbook

1. Inventory what you have

List how each service configures its SDK today: environment variables, code, agent flags. You will usually find a few patterns that cover most services, and a long tail of one-offs.

2. Check language support

Support varies by language and by feature. The project tracks it in the specification compliance matrix and the configuration repository's language support status13. Start with the languages where support is mature in your stack.

3. Write a small set of standard files

Create a baseline per service type, such as web API, worker and batch job, covering resource attributes, exporters to your Collector gateway, batching, sampling and views. Keep secrets and endpoints as substitutions.

4. Ship the file with the platform, not the app

Mount it from a ConfigMap or bake it into base images, and set OTEL_CONFIG_FILE in your deployment templates. Teams inherit good defaults without copying settings.

5. Validate in CI

The model is defined by a JSON schema, so files can be validated before they ship3. Add the check to the same pipeline that enforces admission policies.

6. Migrate service by service

Run the declarative file alongside existing settings in a non-production environment, compare the telemetry produced, then switch. Pay attention to resource attributes and sampling, where small differences change dashboards and costs.

7. Plan for deprecations

The project intends to deprecate environment variables that don't interoperate well with declarative configuration, while making clear that deprecation is not deletion16. Moving now avoids a rushed migration later.

Where to be careful

  • Precedence. Understand how the file interacts with remaining environment variables in each language before assuming one wins.
  • Instrumentation configuration. The API for configuring instrumentation through the model was out of scope for the initial stabilisation1; check what your language supports.
  • Runtime changes. Dynamic configuration, changing telemetry without a restart, is still being designed1.
  • Stability is per language. A stable schema doesn't mean every SDK implementation is stable yet; follow the same approach as stable by default.

How I can help

I design observability platforms where telemetry is configured once, centrally and consistently, from SDK to Collector to backend. As a fractional CTO I can own that roadmap. Or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: AI-assisted claims triage that adjusters trust and regulators can audit
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a US insurer can triage first notice of loss with AI while keeping adjusters in control: document extraction, routing, fraud signals and an auditable AI programme.
item.content:encoded:
Claims arrive as phone notes, emails, photos and PDFs. Triage decides which adjuster sees what, how fast, and with which flags. The goal was to use AI to do that first pass well, without letting a model decide anyone's claim, and with a governance programme ready for state regulators.

The situation

A multi-line insurer in the United States handled first notice of loss through a mix of call centre notes, web forms, emails with attachments and broker submissions. Triage was manual: a team read each new claim, decided its complexity, picked a queue and flagged anything suspicious. At peaks, the backlog meant simple claims waited behind complex ones, and the quality of triage depended on who happened to read the file.

Leadership wanted AI in the loop. The claims and compliance teams wanted something else first: confidence that no model would quietly decide a claim, and evidence they could show a regulator about how AI was governed.

What had to be true

  • Adjusters decide. AI summarises, extracts and suggests; coverage, payment and denial decisions stay with licensed staff.
  • Every flag has a reason a person can read and challenge.
  • Testing for error and unfair outcomes before release and on a schedule, by line of business.
  • One inventory of AI systems with owners, purpose, data and controls.
  • No change to the claims system of record; AI writes suggestions alongside it, not into it.

These map closely to the NAIC model bulletin, which asks insurers to maintain a written programme for the responsible use of AI systems, including governance, risk management controls and testing for errors, bias and unfair discrimination1. A growing number of states have adopted it, so building to it was the safest baseline across jurisdictions23.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

Extraction used structured outputs validated against a schema, so a malformed response fails fast rather than reaching an adjuster, the pattern described in structured outputs for reliable LLM integration. Fraud signals drew on relationships between parties, addresses, repairers and prior claims, using the graph approach in entity resolution for knowledge graphs.

The hard part: fairness and explainability, not extraction

Getting a model to read a claim form well is now the easy part. The difficult questions were about outcomes. Does a fraud signal fire more often for claims from certain postcodes for reasons unrelated to fraud? Does a severity hint systematically under-prioritise one line of business? The bulletin expects insurers to test for exactly these risks1, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework gave a practical structure for mapping, measuring and managing them4.

  • An evaluation set of historical claims with known outcomes, refreshed regularly, scored for extraction accuracy and routing agreement.
  • Outcome comparisons across segments the compliance team defined, reviewed before each release.
  • Fraud signals limited to features the special investigations team could explain, with every flag showing its contributing reasons.
  • Override rates tracked by signal; a signal adjusters routinely override gets investigated, not ignored.

Adjuster overrides are the most valuable data in a claims AI programme. They show, in real time, where the model and the experts disagree.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
AI suggests, adjusters decideStraight-through automationKeeps accountability with licensed staff and simplifies regulatory answers
Rules for complexity, models for readingOne end-to-end modelRouting logic stays readable and changeable by claims ops
Shadow mode firstLaunch with suggestions liveMeasured agreement before influencing anyone
Explainable fraud featuresOpaque anomaly scoresInvestigators can act on, and challenge, a reason
Build to the NAIC bulletin everywhereState-by-state variantsOne programme, mapped to each state's adoption

For insurers with European operations, the EU AI Act adds another layer: its Annex III lists AI used for risk assessment and pricing of natural persons in life and health insurance as high-risk5. Claims triage sits next to that boundary, so classification should be confirmed with counsel; the governance described here is a strong starting point either way. See ISO 42001 vs the NIST AI RMF and Colorado's AI law reset for the wider landscape.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: write the AI programme and the evaluation set before writing the first prompt, and run in shadow mode. Differently: involve the special investigations team in designing fraud signals from the first week. Their sense of what makes a signal actionable shaped the design more than any model choice.

item.title: Giving a fast-moving seed team the technical leadership investors expect at Series A
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a part-time CTO helped a seed-stage team set a technical roadmap, decision records, delivery metrics, SLOs, security foundations and its first senior hires.
item.content:encoded:
Founders shipping quickly, customers arriving, and a Series A process ahead. Architecture decisions lived in chat threads, security questionnaires were piling up and nobody owned hiring for senior engineers. The goal was technical leadership that fitted the stage: enough structure to scale and pass scrutiny, without slowing the team down.

The situation

A seed-stage B2B software company had found traction. The founders were strong builders and the small engineering team shipped quickly, but the things that matter at the next stage were falling behind. Architecture choices were made in chat and forgotten, the release process depended on one person, there was no shared view of reliability, and enterprise prospects were sending security questionnaires nobody had time to answer well. A Series A process was on the horizon, and technical diligence would follow.

The company did not yet need, or want to pay for, a full-time CTO. It needed senior technical leadership for part of each week, with a clear plan for handing over.

What had to be true

  • A roadmap the team believed, connecting product goals to platform work and technical debt.
  • Decisions written down, so they can be reviewed, challenged and learned by new hires.
  • Delivery and reliability measured, as signals for improvement rather than targets to game.
  • Security that stands up to scrutiny, with controls and evidence rather than promises.
  • A team that outlasts the engagement: senior hires and habits that keep working after hand-off.

Architecture

Here the architecture was as much the operating model as the system. The technical work rested on a light set of leadership practices, each producing an artefact the team and investors could see.

Architecture decision records followed the lightweight format Michael Nygard described: context, decision and consequences, kept with the code1. How I use them in a fractional role is in architecture decision records for fractional CTOs.

The data flow, end to end

The cadence mattered more than any single document. Each cycle followed the same loop:

Delivery was tracked with DORA's software delivery metrics, which cover throughput and instability. DORA itself warns against turning them into blanket targets, so they were used per service and only to find bottlenecks2. See DORA metrics for AI-assisted engineering. Reliability used a small number of SLOs on the journeys customers cared about, with an agreed policy for what happens when an error budget is spent3.

The hard part: adding structure without slowing the team

A fast seed team is right to be suspicious of process. Every practice had to earn its place by saving more time than it cost. That meant:

  • ADRs only for decisions that are expensive to reverse, written in under an hour, not for every library choice.
  • Automating the evidence: delivery metrics from the pipeline, access reviews from the identity provider, change history from pull requests.
  • Sequencing security work against real demand. The SOC 2 trust services criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy) gave the structure4, with security controls first because every enterprise questionnaire asked about them. More in SOC 2 for AI startups.
  • Hiring senior engineers who could own areas, not just add capacity, so leadership could be handed over rather than borrowed.

A fractional CTO succeeds when the role becomes unnecessary. The test is whether decisions, metrics and hiring keep happening well in the weeks you are not there.

How the engagement ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Fractional CTO firstHire full-time CTO immediatelySenior judgement now, while the company learns what role it needs
ADRs in the repositoryWiki pages or chat threadsVersioned with code, reviewed like code, found by new hires
Metrics as signalsMetrics as targetsAvoids gaming; focuses on bottlenecks
Security controls before certificationRush to an auditReal controls and evidence first; audit when customers require it
Senior owners before headcountHire for capacityCreates leaders who can take over from the fractional role

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: write decisions down from the first week and keep the cadence predictable, even when the week is busy. Differently: start the search for the permanent engineering leader earlier. Good senior hires take longer than any technical workstream, and the hand-off is only as strong as the person receiving it.

item.title: Testing whether an AI company's technology is what the deck says it is
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a structured technical due diligence tested an AI company's architecture, model and data provenance, security, costs and team, ending in a risk-rated report.
item.content:encoded:
An investor was close to committing to a company whose value rested on its AI. The questions were simple to state and hard to answer: is the AI really theirs, do they have the rights to the data behind it, will it scale at a sensible cost, and can this team keep building it?

The situation

A private equity investor was preparing to invest in a software company whose growth story rested on AI: models that automated part of its customers' work and data assets that, the deck said, competitors could not replicate. The commercial and financial diligence was well under way. What the deal team lacked was an independent view of whether the technology, the data rights and the team matched the story, and what it would cost to fix anything that did not.

The timeline was set by the deal, so the review had to be structured, evidence-led and focused on findings that could change price, terms or the post-close plan.

What had to be true

  • Evidence over assertion: every finding tied to something inspected, not only something said in an interview.
  • Proprietary versus borrowed made explicit: which capabilities the company built, and which depend on third-party models or APIs.
  • Data rights traced from source to model to product, including customer data used for training.
  • Costs that scale: inference and cloud spend modelled against the growth plan.
  • A report the deal team can use: risk-rated, with recommended responses, readable by non-engineers.

Architecture

The review was organised into workstreams, each with its own evidence requests and interview plan. AI governance was assessed against the functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (govern, map, measure, manage)1, with ISO/IEC 42001 used as the reference for what a management system for AI looks like2. The comparison is in ISO 42001 vs NIST AI RMF.

The data flow, end to end

Secure development practices were reviewed against the NIST Secure Software Development Framework, which groups practices into preparing the organisation, protecting the software, producing well-secured software and responding to vulnerabilities3. The full checklist I use is in the AI startup technical due diligence checklist, and supply chain questions in AI model supply chain security.

The hard part: proving data rights, not just data

Showing that a company has data is easy. Showing that it may use that data for the purpose the plan depends on is not. The provenance workstream asked, for each dataset behind a model:

  • Where it came from, under which contract or licence, and whether that permits training and commercial use.
  • Whether customer data was used to train shared models, and whether customer contracts allow it.
  • Whether the dataset is documented in a form like a datasheet, covering motivation, composition and collection4.
  • Whether models carry documentation of intended use and evaluation, in the spirit of model cards5.

Regulation was mapped to where the company sells. For customers in the European Union, the review considered how the EU AI Act might classify the product and which provider or deployer obligations could apply6.

In AI diligence, the most valuable finding is often not a technical flaw but a missing right. A gap in data permissions can matter more to value than any code quality issue.

How the engagement ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Scope to the deal thesisExhaustive technical auditEffort goes to what can change price or terms
Repository accessDocuments and interviews onlyInspection gives stronger evidence than representation
Dedicated provenance workstreamFold into legal reviewData rights need technical tracing, not only contract reading
Recognised frameworks as referenceAd hoc checklistFindings are comparable and defensible
Recommended response per findingList of issuesDeal team can act: price, condition, warranty or plan

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: insist on repository and billing access early, and separate verified findings from representations in the report. Differently: start the data rights tracing on the first day, in parallel with legal counsel. It is the slowest workstream and the one most likely to change the deal.

item.title: From many monitoring tools to one view of what customers experience
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a telecom operator consolidated monitoring with OpenTelemetry, a collector gateway, eBPF instrumentation and SLO burn-rate alerting tied to customer journeys.
item.content:encoded:
Many monitoring tools, each owned by a different team, and incidents still reported by customers before anyone inside noticed. The goal was one telemetry pipeline, service-level objectives tied to customer journeys, and alerts that fire because users are affected rather than because a server is busy.

The situation

A telecom operator ran customer-facing digital services (self-care apps, online ordering, payments and activation) on top of a mix of modern microservices and long-lived back-office systems. Monitoring had grown team by team. Each group had its own agents, dashboards and alert rules, and the same incident lit up several tools at once without any of them saying whether customers were affected.

The pattern on bad days was familiar: complaints arrived through support channels first, several teams investigated in parallel from their own dashboards, and the root cause sat at a boundary nobody's tool covered.

What had to be true

  • One vendor-neutral telemetry pipeline, so instrumentation is done once and backends can change.
  • Traces across boundaries, from the app request through the API layer to the back-office call.
  • Objectives tied to customer journeys, agreed with the people who own those journeys.
  • Alerts that mean action: page when users are being hurt, ticket when a budget is slowly eroding, and nothing else.
  • Cost under control, with sampling and cardinality managed centrally rather than service by service.

Architecture

The core was an OpenTelemetry Collector gateway: services and node-level agents send OTLP to a central endpoint per cluster or region, where processing, sampling and export happen once1. Deployment patterns are compared in OpenTelemetry Collector deployment patterns.

For older services that could not be changed quickly, OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation (OBI) captured spans and rate, error and duration metrics for HTTP and gRPC traffic without code changes2. It cannot see business context, so revenue-critical services also received SDK instrumentation for custom attributes. More in OpenTelemetry eBPF instrumentation.

The data flow, end to end

Prometheus held the SLI time series and evaluated recording and alerting rules, which suits numeric operational data well, though not anything that needs exact per-request accounting3.

The hard part: deciding what to promise

The pipeline was engineering. The objectives were negotiation. Each journey (sign in, view bill, pay, activate) needed an indicator measured close to the user, a target the business could defend, and an owner who accepted the consequences of the error budget5. In practice that meant:

  • Choosing indicators at the edge of the journey, not on internal components that customers never see.
  • Starting with targets the service already met most of the time, then tightening, rather than declaring aspirational numbers nobody could hold.
  • Writing a short error budget policy per journey that said what happens when the budget runs low.
  • Retiring old component alerts deliberately, with each team agreeing what replaced them.

Alerting followed the multiwindow, multi-burn-rate approach in the Google SRE Workbook, which pairs a long window for significance with a short window for fast reset4. The practical version for smaller teams is in SLOs and error budgets for small teams.

An SLO is a business decision expressed in numbers. If product owners have not agreed it, it is just another threshold.

How the engagement ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
OpenTelemetry and OTLPVendor agents per toolInstrument once; backends become replaceable
Collector gatewayServices export directlyCentral sampling, filtering and credentials
OBI for legacy servicesWait for code changesBaseline traces now; SDKs where context matters
Journey-level SLOsPer-component thresholdsAlerts reflect customer impact, not resource noise
Multiwindow burn-rate alertsStatic error-rate alertsBetter precision and faster reset

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: trace one journey end to end before instrumenting everything, and make product owners co-own the targets. Differently: set attribute naming and cardinality rules before the first service onboards. Cleaning up inconsistent labels later cost more than agreeing them early.

item.title: Automating lease, ID and invoice intake without letting a model write to the ledger
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a property operator replaced manual keying of leases, IDs and invoices with schema-validated AI extraction, confidence thresholds and exception queues.
item.content:encoded:
Leases, identity documents and supplier invoices arrived as scans, photos and PDFs, and every one was keyed in by hand before a tenant could be onboarded or a bill paid. The goal was to automate the routine documents and make the rest faster to check, while keeping the core system's data trustworthy.

The situation

A property operator onboarded tenants and paid suppliers through a core property management system. Everything that fed it arrived as documents: signed leases, identity documents, proof of address, supplier invoices and service contracts. Each was opened, read and keyed by hand. Onboarding waited on the queue, keying errors surfaced later as billing disputes, and the team spent its time transcribing rather than checking.

Earlier attempts with template-based OCR had struggled because the documents varied too much: different lease templates, scanned and photographed IDs, and invoices in every layout a supplier could invent.

What had to be true

  • Every value validated before it reaches the core system, by rules the business can read.
  • The model never writes: it proposes a record, and deterministic code decides what is posted.
  • Uncertain documents go to people, with the reason and the source region visible.
  • Personal data handled deliberately: limited access, defined retention and no identity documents in logs or prompts beyond what extraction needs.
  • Traceability from any posted value back to the page it came from.

Architecture

Each document type had a versioned JSON Schema describing its fields, types, formats and required properties1. The model was asked to return output conforming to that schema, and the same schema validated the response, so a malformed answer failed loudly instead of slipping through. More on the pattern in structured outputs for reliable LLM integration.

The data flow, end to end

The audit and staging tables in Postgres carried their own check, not-null and foreign key constraints, so invalid states were rejected by the database as well as by the application3. Retries were safe because posting was idempotent, the same discipline described in idempotent payment and order pipelines.

The hard part: confidence you can act on

Extraction quality was rarely the blocker. Deciding when to trust it was. A model's own statement of certainty is not a reliable signal, so confidence was built from evidence instead:

  • Arithmetic and consistency checks: invoice lines must sum to totals, lease dates must be in order, rent schedules must match the term.
  • Reference checks: the unit, tenant or supplier must exist and match what the document claims.
  • Field-level thresholds set per document type from a labelled sample, with stricter rules on fields that move money or identify people.
  • Reason codes on every exception, so the team could see which rule or field caused most reviews and fix the cause.

Documents are also untrusted input. Text inside an uploaded file can carry instructions aimed at the model, a form of indirect prompt injection2. The defence was architectural: the extraction model had no tools and no credentials, its output was confined to the schema, and posting was done by code that ignored anything outside defined fields. See prompt injection defence.

The model is the least trusted component in the pipeline. Design so that the worst it can do is produce a record that fails validation.

How the engagement ran

Ongoing monitoring of exception rates, corrections and drift by document type followed the measure-and-manage approach of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework4.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Vision LLM with schemasTemplate OCR per layoutHandles layout variety without a template for every supplier
Deterministic postingAgent with system accessModel holds no credentials; injection cannot cause writes
Evidence-based confidenceModel self-reported scoresThresholds grounded in checks and measured error rates
Reason-coded exceptionsGeneric review queueShows which rule or field to improve next
Versioned schemas per typeOne generic document schemaClear validation and safe, reviewable change

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: keep the model away from credentials and let validation, not the model, decide what is posted. Differently: build the labelled sample before the pipeline. Every threshold discussion went faster once there was a shared set of real documents to measure against.

item.title: Making a decades-old media archive findable with model enrichment and a controlled vocabulary
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a media archive made decades of content findable: batch model enrichment mapped to a SKOS vocabulary, human review queues and semantic search with provenance.
item.content:encoded:
A large archive of video, audio and photographs, catalogued under decades of changing conventions, with most items described by little more than a title and a date. The goal was consistent, searchable metadata at archive scale, without letting a model invent the catalogue.

The situation

A media organisation held decades of video, audio and photography. The material was valuable for new programmes, licensing and research, but most of it was hard to find. Cataloguing conventions had changed several times, many items carried only a title and a broadcast date, and the same subject was described in a dozen ways. Search worked if you already knew the exact words a cataloguer had used years earlier, and otherwise depended on a few long-serving people who remembered where things were.

The organisation wanted to use AI to describe the backlog. The concern, rightly, was that a model left to itself would produce confident, inconsistent tags at a scale nobody could review.

What had to be true

  • One controlled vocabulary, so a subject, place or person is described the same way across the archive.
  • Machine suggestions, human authority: models propose, people decide where confidence is low or the subject is sensitive.
  • Provenance on every field, so anyone can see whether a label came from a cataloguer, a model or a reviewer.
  • Search by meaning and by exact term, for editors who know what they want and for those who are exploring.
  • A taxonomy the archive team owns, not one hidden inside prompts or code.

Architecture

The vocabulary was modelled as a SKOS concept scheme, which gives each concept a preferred label, alternative labels and broader or narrower relationships1. Descriptive fields such as creator, date, subject and rights were aligned with DCMI Metadata Terms so that records stayed portable between systems2.

The data flow, end to end

For semantic search, transcripts and summaries were embedded with a sentence-embedding model, which produces vectors that can be compared with cosine similarity3. Nearest-neighbour lookup used an HNSW index, a graph-based approximate search method that scales well to large collections4. Model choice and storage trade-offs are covered in choosing embedding models and pgvector or a vector database.

The hard part: a vocabulary people agree on

Running models over the archive was the easy part. Agreeing what the labels should be took far longer. The approach that worked:

  • Seed the concept scheme from the terms cataloguers already used most, then merge duplicates as alternative labels rather than deleting them, so old records still match.
  • Use SKOS mapping properties to link local concepts to external vocabularies where they existed, instead of copying those vocabularies wholesale1.
  • Never let the pipeline create a concept. A model suggestion with no match becomes a proposal for the taxonomy owner, with example items attached.
  • Treat people and sensitive topics as always-reviewed fields, whatever the model's confidence.

The taxonomy design choices are discussed further in SKOS vs OWL for enterprise taxonomies.

A controlled vocabulary turns a model from an author into an assistant. The model can only choose from concepts people have agreed, and everything else becomes a question for a person.

How the engagement ran

Thresholds were set against a hand-labelled evaluation set drawn from the pilot collection, not against the model's own sense of certainty. The method is in LLM evaluation sets that predict production.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
SKOS concept schemeFree-text model tagsConsistent labels, synonyms and hierarchy; reusable outside the pipeline
Batch enrichmentReal-time tagging on viewPredictable cost, reproducible runs and reviewable outputs
Structured model outputsProse descriptions parsed laterFields validate on arrival; failures are visible, not silent
Review by confidence and sensitivityReview everything, or nothingPeople spend time where the model is weakest or the risk is highest
Hybrid keyword and vector searchVector search onlyEditors still need exact names, dates and identifiers

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put the vocabulary at the centre and make provenance a field, not a log file. Differently: involve the cataloguers in designing the review screen from the first week. The speed and quality of review decided the throughput of the whole system, far more than the model did.

item.title: Building an AI tutor that teaches the syllabus instead of doing the homework
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an education platform built an AI tutor grounded in its syllabus: curriculum retrieval, guided hints instead of answers, safety filters and teacher dashboards.
item.content:encoded:
Generic chatbots gave students answers that ignored the syllabus, skipped the reasoning and pitched the language at the wrong age. The goal was a tutor grounded in the curriculum, that guides with hints rather than handing over answers, stays safe for young learners and shows teachers where students are stuck.

The situation

An education platform served structured courses to school-age students, aligned to a defined syllabus. Students were already using general-purpose chatbots for homework help, and teachers could see the result: correct answers with methods the class had never been taught, explanations pitched at university level, and no sign the student had learned anything. The platform wanted its own tutor, built around how its courses actually teach, and one that teachers could see into and trust rather than work around.

What had to be true

  • Grounded in the syllabus: the same methods, notation and vocabulary as the lessons.
  • Teaches, not tells: hints and questions first, with solutions only where the teaching design allows.
  • Safe for the age range, on what students type and on what the tutor says.
  • Useful to teachers, as insight into misconceptions rather than transcripts to read.
  • Affordable at classroom scale, when a whole year group logs in at once.

UNESCO's guidance on generative AI in education calls for data privacy protections, an age limit for independent use and validation of tools for pedagogical and ethical suitability1. Those became design inputs, not an afterthought: the tutor was designed for supervised use within the platform, with schools in control of access.

Architecture

Grounding followed the retrieval-augmented generation pattern, combining a model with retrieval from a specific corpus2, here the platform's own lessons and worked examples filtered by the student's course and unit. See the RAG to production checklist.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: hinting without leaking the answer

Getting a model to be helpful is easy. Getting it to be helpful in the right way, and to resist a determined student asking for "just the answer" five different ways, is the real work.

  • The tutoring policy was explicit and versioned: which exercise types allow worked solutions, how many hints before a fuller explanation, when to ask the student to show their step.
  • Teachers authored a misconception library per objective, so hints targeted the likely error rather than repeating the method.
  • An output check compared tutor responses against the exercise's answer key to catch leaked final answers.
  • Attempts to override the tutor's instructions were treated as expected behaviour, not edge cases; prompt injection is the first entry in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications4. See prompt injection defence.

The best tutor response is often a question. Evaluate for that explicitly, because a model left alone will optimise for being helpful in the moment.

How the engagement ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Retrieve from own curriculumRely on model knowledgeMatches taught methods, notation and level
Explicit tutoring policy"Be a good tutor" promptTestable behaviour per exercise type
Guardrails on input and outputOutput filtering onlyProtects students and the tutor's instructions
Prompt caching on stable prefixFull prompt every turnLower cost and latency at peak load
Events, not transcripts, for teachersTeachers read chatsInsight at class level; less exposure of student text

Tutoring prompts share a long, stable prefix of instructions, policy and lesson context. Prompt caching reuses a processed prompt prefix across requests, so only the changing tail is processed fresh, and any change to the prefix is a cache miss3. Structuring prompts so the stable parts come first made caching effective. Details in prompt caching for cost and latency.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: write the tutoring policy with teachers before writing prompts, and let teachers grade the test set. Differently: build the teacher dashboard earlier. Seeing where whole classes got stuck changed the content roadmap as much as the tutor.

item.title: Helping lawyers review contracts against the playbook without giving up the final word
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a legal team moved from manual playbook checks to AI-assisted review: structured clause extraction, playbook comparison and cited suggestions lawyers accept.
item.content:encoded:
Every incoming contract was compared to the playbook by hand, clause by clause, under deadline. The goal was not to replace that judgement but to prepare it: extract the clauses, compare them to the playbook, and propose cited redlines a lawyer accepts, edits or rejects.

The situation

A legal team handled a steady flow of commercial agreements: supplier contracts, NDAs, services agreements, licences. Each one was checked against an internal playbook that set out preferred positions, acceptable fallbacks and red lines for clauses such as liability caps, indemnities, termination, governing law and data protection. The work was skilled but repetitive, and it bunched up at quarter end when everything was urgent.

The team had tried generic AI chat tools. The answers sounded plausible, cited nothing, and didn't know the playbook. Nobody trusted them, rightly.

What had to be true

  • The lawyer decides. The system prepares and proposes; it never sends a redline on its own.
  • Every suggestion is cited to the exact contract text and the playbook position it relies on.
  • Consistent structure, so outputs can be validated and compared, not just read.
  • Measured accuracy per clause type, on the team's own contracts, before anyone relies on it.
  • Confidentiality: contract text handled under the firm's existing data controls.

Contract review is a well-studied task: the CUAD dataset, built with legal experts, frames it as finding the clauses a reviewer needs to see across dozens of categories1. That framing, extraction first and judgement second, shaped the design.

Architecture

Extraction used structured outputs, where the model's response is constrained to a supplied JSON Schema2. Each clause came back with its type, section reference, verbatim quote and confidence. A deterministic check then confirmed that every quote actually appeared in the source document. See structured outputs for reliable LLM integration.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: long context versus retrieval

A single contract usually fits within a modern model's context window, so the temptation is to put everything in: the contract, the whole playbook, and a pile of precedents. Research on long contexts shows models use information at the start and end of the input more reliably than information in the middle3, which is a poor property when the clause that matters is on page fourteen.

The design split the jobs:

  • The contract is read whole for extraction, because cross-references and definitions matter.
  • The playbook is retrieved per clause, in the spirit of retrieval-augmented generation4, so each comparison sees only the relevant positions.
  • Comparison runs clause by clause, with small, focused prompts that are easier to evaluate.

The trade-offs are covered in long context vs RAG.

Contracts from counterparties are also untrusted input. Prompt injection tops the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications5, so contract text was always treated as data, the model had no tools that could act on it, and outputs were constrained by schema. See prompt injection defence.

A suggestion a lawyer can verify in ten seconds is worth more than a fluent paragraph they have to check from scratch.

How the engagement ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Structured extraction firstFree-text review in one promptValidatable, comparable, displayable output
Verbatim quotes checked in codeTrust the model's quotesCatches fabricated or paraphrased citations
Playbook as structured positionsPlaybook document in the promptPrecise retrieval; easier to maintain
Evaluation per clause typeOne overall accuracy figureStrong clause types ship; weak ones wait
Lawyer decides every suggestionAuto-apply high-confidence redlinesAccountability stays with the profession

Building evaluation sets that hold up in production is covered in evaluation sets that predict production.

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: turn the playbook into data before writing a prompt, and treat lawyer decisions as the evaluation signal. Differently: involve lawyers in schema design from the start. The clause taxonomy is a legal decision, and the earlier they own it, the fewer rework cycles follow.
